text.p: British pension funds on Monday said they were nervous about possible early government moves to scale back on industry tax benefits in the budget.

They said Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, already with a reputation for swift action after a month in the job, could reduce relief available through Advance Corporation Tax, or scrap it altogether when he delivers his budget on July 2.

A complete scrapping is considered unlikely but funds say they cannot rule it out given Brown's surprise moves to give the Bank of England autonomy in setting interest rates and revamping regulation of the City.
"I expect he will look to cut ACT relief, probably to 10 percent. He is unlikely to go much further," said a senior director of a fund management group.
ACT is currently set at 20 percent and is levied from a company's gross profits at the same time as dividends are paid to shareholders.
It can be offset against a company's corporation tax liability, which means that it does not increase a company's overall tax burden.

Tax-exempt organisations such as pension funds benefit from a higher rate of ACT because they can claim more cash back from the government, so they would bear the financial brunt of any plans to drop the rate.

There is a precedent for increasing revenue by lowering ACT. In 1993, Chancellor Norman Lamont lowered the ACT rate to 20 percent from 25 percent, a move which raised an extra billion sterling in government revenue.
An abolition of ACT relief is estimated to be worth about five billion sterling to the Treasury.

The director said the move was likely to be a relatively easy one to push through given the lack of an obvious immediate victim, although the industry has stressed that changes would effectively be most keenly felt by the individual pensioner.

In an attempt to pre-empt changes, many investment trusts, including four in the Kleinwort Benson Investment Management stable, the Dunedin Enterprise Fund and the Invesco Blue Chip and Recovery funds, have brought forward their dividend payments.

One investment trust manager, who asked not to be identified, said the move to bring forward dividend payments was precautionary, and may not have its desired effect as Brown could backdate any changes to the beginning of the tax year.
"But there is nothing to lose by doing it," he said.
The National Association of Pension Funds has been lobbying hard against any reduction in relief, and believes it has made Brown aware of the consequences of such a move.

NAPF director of investment services John Rogers said an ACT reduction would reduce industry competitiveness as companies will have to make up shortfalls in pension fund income relatively quickly, thus diverting money away from investment.

"It is still a big concern. (The pension fund lobby) hasn't won any concessions but we do know that the point has been taken so that if the government decides to cut pension fund income they will know the implications of that. There is no doubt about that."

He said Brown did have other options open to him, and hoped that the planned windfall tax on privatised utilities would be enough to fill the immediate funding hole created by Labour's election pledge not to raise corporation or income tax.
Blake Dempster, chief executive of Liberty International Pensions, said broader reform of the UK pension system was unlikely in the budget, but in time should come through.
Among these would be moves to encourage compulsory private sector pension provision, which he said would be undermined by a reduced level of ACT. Any ACT changes were likely to be gradual, he said.
Another UK fund manager said the market was not expecting an abolition of relief, although it had been discounting a reduction.

"But then I don't think the market was expecting him to give independence to the Bank of England or take away their responsibilities for regulating the banking sector so we should perhaps expect the unexpected."
